newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN refugee chief wants lifelines to east Zaire.
newsitem.headline: UN refugee chief wants lifelines to east Zaire.

text.p: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata on Sunday appealed for urgent action to open "emergency lifelines" to well over a million people fleeing fighting in eastern Zaire.

In a statement issued from the Geneva headquarters of her UNHCR agency, she also said she was despatching her deputy, Sergio Vieira de Mello, to Rwanda and Zaire to discuss with top officials of both sides ways of easing the crisis.

"This may be a final appeal to all those involved in this terrible conflict, or it will be too late," declared Ogata, a former Japanese university professor who has won widespread respect in her six years as U.N. refugee chief.
"Combatants should stop attacking refugees. The refugees from the largest camps in the region are on the move towards some of the most inhospitable and inaccessible areas in Zaire.
"The further the refugees move west, the more difficult it will be for us to reach them. It may make repatriation and reconciliation impossible."

The UNHCR says some 1.2 million refugees from Rwanda and Burundi -- mainly Hutus fleeing conflict in their own countries -- and tens of thousands of Zairians have been displaced in the eastern Zaire fighting.

It broke out late last month when Zairians of the Tutsi tribe -- which controls the governments in both Rwanda and Burundi -- rose in revolt after Zairian officials indicated they wanted to expel them.

Zaire, whose President Mobuto Sese Seka has been in Switzerland undergoing cancer treatment since August, accuses Rwanda of sending in troops to back the rebels, who now control large part of eastern Zaire.
The UNHCR, which has been looking after the mainly Hutu occupants of teeming refugee camps in the region, withdrew its last expatriate staff from the area this weekend because of the fighting.

The U.N. agency said that since the conflict broke out in the Uvira and Bakavu regions of eastern Zaire two weeks ago it had had no contact at all with the some 520,000 Burundi and Rwanda refugees there.

"We must open emergency lifelines to the refugees and displaced people now, wherever they are. We must open humanitarian corridoors to enable refugees to return in safety to Rwanda and Burundi," Ogata declared in her statement.
"Unless we reach the refugees soon, many women and children, the elderly, the sick and the wounded are going to die."
She issued the appeal within hours of returning to Geneva to handle the crisis, cutting short a visit to the U.N. General Assembly in New York.
She did not specify how she believed the corridors should be opened, but there seemed little doubt she wanted the major powers to take some urgent action.

Most of the Rwandan Hutu refugees in eastern Zaire, as well as others in Tanzania and Burundi, fled their home country after the 1994 genocide in which up to a million Tutsis were killed by Hutu mobs, soldiers and militia.
In the wake of the genocide, the Tutsi-led Rwanda Patriotic Front took power in the country and leaders of the previous Hutu administration fled with the refugees.
